claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a low intrinsic Mn content.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a uniform microstructure and low Mn segregation.
Oxidizing annealing at 200–300 °C for 2–4 hours enhances Mn diffusion to the near-surface region of Q235 steel.
Oxidizing annealing at 200–300 °C for 2–4 hours promotes Mn segregation to Q235 grain boundaries.
Oxidizing annealing forms a Mn-rich surface oxide on Q235 steel.
The resulting Mn-rich oxide layer is continuous.
The degree of Mn segregation governs the structure and continuity of the oxide film.
A continuous Mn-rich oxide suppresses corrosion of Q235 steel in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
The Mn-rich layer can act sacrificially and thereby protect the underlying alloy.
Mn can modify the local electrochemical environment to reduce anodic dissolution.
Inert annealing minimizes Mn migration and leaves the Mn distribution similar to untreated Q235 steel.
Inert-annealed Q235 steel has corrosion behavior comparable to untreated Q235 steel.
Segregated Mn regions may act as cathodic sites and produce distinct pitting patterns.
The low intrinsic Mn content of Q235 may limit Mn segregation and formation of an influential continuous oxide film.
The proposed Mn-mediated effect applies in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at room temperature and 80 °C after annealing at 200–300 °C.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts corrosion suppression by oxidizing annealing, but the predicted outcome also permits cathodic Mn regions and distinct pitting rather than suppression, leaving the directional prediction internally inconsistent.
The initial state is described as uniform and as having a low natural segregation profile, whereas the mechanism describes the untreated-like Mn distribution as heterogeneous.
